<section class="book-reviews-section page-has-custom-h1">
  <div class="container">
    <div class="reviews-intro">
      <h1>Book Reviews</h1>
      <p class="page-subtitle">Critical reviews of golf science, biomechanics, and nonlinear control literature</p>
      <p>
        In-depth reviews examining the mathematical foundations, biomechanical insights,
        and modeling assumptions of key texts, evaluated against the control-affine AffineDrift framework.
      </p>
    </div>

    <section class="planned-reviews u-mt-4">
      <h2>Foundational Literature Reviews</h2>
      <div class="reviews-list">

        <article class="review-card">
          <div class="review-header">
            <h2>The Search for the Perfect Swing</h2>
            <span class="review-date">A. Cochran &amp; J. Stobbs, 1968</span>
          </div>
          <div class="review-content">
            <p>
              Cochran and Stobbs' seminal text represents the foundational quantitative investigation into golf swing mechanics.
              Commissioned by the Golf Society of Great Britain, the study introduced the planar double-pendulum representation
              (hub/torso segment driving a distal club segment) that established early analytical benchmarks for kinetic energy transfer
              and clubhead speed generation.
            </p>
            <p>
              <strong>AffineDrift Analysis:</strong> The classical double-pendulum model captures the dominant passive inertial coupling
              that accelerates the distal segment during late downswing. However, modern control-affine analysis demonstrates that treating
              the hub as a fixed axle understates the role of moving-base reaction wrenches and bilateral hand constraints.
              While Cochran &amp; Stobbs assumed pure parametric release, the AffineDrift framework formalizes this as an underactuated drift trajectory
              where proximal deceleration is an emergent consequence of dynamic coupling rather than active muscular braking.
            </p>
          </div>
        </article>

        <article class="review-card">
          <div class="review-header">
            <h2>The Physics of Golf</h2>
            <span class="review-date">A. Raymond Penner, 2003 (Rep. Prog. Phys. 66:131–171)</span>
          </div>
          <div class="review-content">
            <p>
              Penner's comprehensive review provides rigorous analytical treatments spanning club-head aerodynamics, oblique impact dynamics,
              and flexible shaft modal behavior. His parametric models established standard mathematical formulations for the launch conditions
              resulting from normal and tangential contact compliance.
            </p>
            <p>
              <strong>AffineDrift Analysis:</strong> Penner's modal expansion for shaft deflection provides crucial empirical constraints
              for validating the elastic modes in the Zero-Torque Counterfactual (ZTCF) framework. By isolating the conservative elastic energy
              stored during transition from active hand-applied wrench work, Penner's findings corroborate that shaft kick at impact contributes
              a predictable, state-dependent velocity increment governed by the system's unforced natural frequencies.
            </p>
          </div>
        </article>

        <article class="review-card">
          <div class="review-header">
            <h2>Underactuated Robotics: Algorithms for Walking, Running, Swimming, Flying, and Manipulation</h2>
            <span class="review-date">Russ Tedrake, MIT OpenCourseWare</span>
          </div>
          <div class="review-content">
            <p>
              Tedrake's course text serves as the modern authority on the mechanics and control of systems where control authority is lower
              than the degrees of freedom ($\dim(u) < \dim(q)$). It develops dynamic programming, trajectory optimization (direct collocation),
              time-varying LQR, transverse coordinates, and funnel mechanics.
            </p>
            <p>
              <strong>AffineDrift Analysis:</strong> The mathematical machinery of AffineDrift—specifically transverse linearization along nominal
              orbits $\delta \dot{x}_\perp = A_\perp(t)\delta x_\perp + B_\perp(t)\delta u$ and region-of-attraction computation via sums-of-squares (SOS)—is
              directly anchored in the methods developed by Tedrake. Applying underactuated robotics to the human swing reframes technique not
              as rigid kinematic tracking, but as stabilization of invariant manifolds in phase space.
            </p>
          </div>

        </article>

      </div>
    </section>
